extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy; readers of Aristotle (Nicomachean Ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading / study of Book 1 of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics (Bekker page 1094a), focusing on Aristotle's account of ends, the Good, and the hierarchy of arts/sciences. Useful for philosophical analysis, teaching, or citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every art and investigation aims at some good
rubrics_metrics.description: Each art, investigation, practical pursuit, or undertaking seems to aim at some good; the Good is that at which all things aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle asserts this as a foundational principle: to understand practices or sciences one should identify the end (the good) they aim at. Use this to analyze any activity by asking what end it seeks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between activities-as-ends and product-as-end
rubrics_metrics.description: Some arts have the activity of practising the art as their end (e.g., flute-playing), whereas others have an end that is a product distinct from the activity (e.g., building aims at a house).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an art or practice, note whether its value lies in the performance itself or in an externally produced object; Aristotle notes that where the end is a product, the product is essentially superior in value to the activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of subordinate and master arts (ends of master arts preferred)
rubrics_metrics.description: When several pursuits are subordinate to a single faculty (e.g., bridle-making subordinate to horsemanship), the ends of the master arts are more to be desired than the ends of subordinate arts because subordinate ends are pursued for the sake of the master end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To understand the relative value or priority of ends, identify if an art is subordinate and trace its end to the master art; the master art's end frames the value of subordinate aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of infinite regress in choosing ends (existence of an ultimate End)
rubrics_metrics.description: If we did not will at least one thing for its own sake (rather than for the sake of something else), desires would lead to an endless regress, making all desire futile; therefore there must be one ultimate End — the Good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a methodological constraint when analyzing aims: posit that analysis should terminate in an ultimate, self-sufficient end (the Supreme Good) rather than an infinite chain of instrumental ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Good is the ultimate End willed for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: The one ultimate End that we will for its own sake, while willing other things only for the sake of this, is the Good and specifically the Supreme Good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In ethical inquiry, identify the ultimate object of practical deliberation (what is chosen for its own sake) and treat it as the focal Good toward which other aims are instrumentally ordered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical importance of knowing the Supreme Good
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of the Supreme Good has practical importance for conduct of life: knowing the proper end better enables us to attain it (Aristotle compares it to archers having a target).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle recommends attempting at least an outline determination of the Supreme Good and which science or faculty has it as its object, because such knowledge guides practical action and policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politics as the master science because it ordains other sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: The supreme End appears to be the object of the most authoritative science — politics — since politics ordains which sciences are to exist in states; thus politics is a pre-eminent master-craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assigning responsibility for the supreme human good or organizing practical aims, consider political science as the overarching practical science that sets communal ends and structures other arts/sciences.
